title: Bullets at the Gym: Bishnoi Gang Shoots Up Guru Randhawa's Delhi Fitness Franchise — Because He's 'Close to Salman Khan'
excerpt: Two masked gunmen targeted the singer's 24HS Fitness gym in Paschim Vihar. No casualties, but the Bishnoi gang's claim of responsibility — and their transnational reach into Canada and the US — makes this more than a Bollywood turf story.
body:
There is a certain kind of story that only Bollywood's security crisis can produce — one where a pop star's gym gets shot up not because of anything he did, but because of who he had dinner with.

On June 11, two masked men on a motorcycle pulled up to 24HS Fitness in Delhi's Paschim Vihar — a gym franchise co-owned by Guru Randhawa — and opened fire. Multiple rounds were discharged. Bullets shattered the glass storefront. Mercifully, nobody was inside at the time of the attack, and there were zero casualties.

<youtube>https://youtube.com/watch?v=fQkzgKtggvg</youtube>


Within hours, the claim of responsibility landed. And it came not from some Delhi street gang, but from a US-based operative.

## The Bishnoi Gang's Facebook Confession

Anil Pandit, a member of the Lawrence Bishnoi gang reportedly based in the United States, took to Facebook to claim the attack. His reasoning was chillingly casual: Guru Randhawa was "getting very close to Salman Khan."

Let that sink in. In 2026, a man based thousands of miles from Delhi can order shots fired at a gym because a singer's social circle displeases a jailed gangster. The Bishnoi gang's operational reach — spanning India, Canada, and the US — has turned Bollywood's security landscape into something out of a transnational thriller that no studio would greenlight for being too implausible.

## A Pattern That Won't Break

This is not an isolated incident. The Bishnoi gang has been escalating its campaign of celebrity intimidation with disturbing regularity:

In January 2026, gunmen fired shots outside Rohit Shetty's Mumbai residence. Kapil Sharma's café in Canada was targeted. And the most devastating strike remains the 2022 murder of Sidhu Moosewala — a killing that sent shockwaves through the global Punjabi community and remains an open wound in diaspora consciousness.

The thread connecting all of these? The Bishnoi-Salman Khan feud, which traces back to the actor's 1998 blackbuck poaching case. Lawrence Bishnoi, currently in jail, has declared that anyone perceived as an ally of Salman Khan is a legitimate target. The definition of "ally" appears to be expansive — and Guru Randhawa, who has performed at Salman's events and been photographed with him socially, apparently qualifies.

## Why NRIs Can't Dismiss This as 'Bollywood Drama'

Here's where the story crosses the ocean.

The Bishnoi gang's diaspora footprint is not theoretical — it is operational. Canada has been a particular concern, with investigations linking gang associates to activities in Ontario and British Columbia. The US connection, now confirmed via Anil Pandit's brazen social media claim, adds another jurisdiction to the map.

For NRIs in North America, this raises uncomfortable questions. Are diaspora communities being used as staging grounds for organised crime operations targeting Indian celebrities? How are these operatives moving money, coordinating attacks, and posting public confessions from abroad without consequence?

Indian intelligence agencies have reportedly flagged the Bishnoi gang's overseas network to their Canadian and American counterparts. But extradition remains painfully slow, and social media platforms have been criticized for allowing threat claims to stay up for hours before removal.

## Guru Randhawa's Response — Or Lack Thereof

As of this writing, Guru Randhawa has not issued a public statement. His social media remains active with promotional content — music videos, brand collaborations, tour dates — as if the shooting never happened. Whether that's strategic composure or genuine shock is anyone's guess.

Delhi Police have registered an FIR and are reviewing CCTV footage from the area. The investigation is ongoing, but given the gang's track record, expectations of a quick resolution are modest.

## The Bigger Question

There was a time when Bollywood's security concerns were limited to overzealous fans and paparazzi scrums. That era is over. The entertainment industry now operates under the shadow of organised crime syndicates with global reach, social media savvy, and an apparent willingness to escalate violence against anyone in their crosshairs — or anyone adjacent to their crosshairs.

Guru Randhawa didn't do anything to the Bishnoi gang. He just knew the wrong person. In today's Bollywood, that's enough to get your gym shot up.

The music industry will move on. Guru Randhawa will release another banger. But the bullets in the glass at 24HS Fitness tell a story that no amount of Punjabi pop can drown out: nobody in Bollywood's orbit is untouchable anymore. And the threat doesn't stop at India's borders.
nri_angle: The Bishnoi gang operates transnationally — Anil Pandit, who claimed responsibility from the US via Facebook, is based overseas. Previous targets include Kapil Sharma's café in Canada. For NRIs, the gang's diaspora footprint turns this into a safety and extradition question, not just Bollywood gossip.
